image.subject: a small team of engineers in casual shirts crowded around a whiteboard covered in sticky notes, all talking at once, no one standing in charge at the front, a bright Silicon Valley office in the late 1990s

storyboard.claim: Early creative work needs open flow with no boss stepping in.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Engineers at a sticky-note whiteboard, nobody in command.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the claim that flat teams foster creativity.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows what the free-flow stage looks like on the ground.

image.subject: a whiteboard split in two, a loose cloud of scribbled ideas on the left and a neat project chart with boxes and owners on the right, in a late-1990s office

storyboard.claim: A company moves from ideation to implementation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Messy ideas on one side of a whiteboard, a structured plan on the other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the creative stage to the next stage.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the implementation phase as a separate job.

image.subject: a young man in his late twenties with tousled brown hair and a casual sweater, thoughtful expression, sitting at a crowded desk buried in printouts and ad reports, looking overloaded while the office hums around him

storyboard.claim: Google scaling AdWords needed managers for implementation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Larry Page at a desk overwhelmed by paper.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the implementation stage to Google.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts a founder in the overloaded position the claim describes.

image.subject: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, sorting colored project cards into rows on the desk between them

storyboard.claim: Implementation requires coordination, which needs managers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager arranging colored cards to coordinate work.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why implementation differs from brainstorming.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows coordination as physical sorting of work.

image.subject: two engineers in hoodies standing in a server room aisle lined with blinking racks, one pointing at a laptop while the other shakes his head, a dispute over which machines go where

storyboard.claim: Without managers, no one allocates servers or breaks ties between engineers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two engineers arguing in front of server racks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives a concrete example of missing coordination.
storyboard.addedInformation: Adds the server rack and the unresolved technical dispute.

left.label: CHAOS
left.subject: a cluttered office with papers spilling off every desk and sticky notes covering the walls

right.label: RIGIDITY
right.subject: a rigid office with identical gray cubicles lined up in perfect rows and a locked filing cabinet

storyboard.claim: Creativity and efficiency pull against each other; both extremes fail.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chaotic office versus rigid office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the tension the previous lines described.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the two failure modes side by side.

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, standing between two small groups of people at a whiteboard with his hands held out level

storyboard.claim: A coach is needed to balance creativity and discipline.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bill Campbell standing between two groups, hands level.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolves the chaos-versus-rigidity tension with a person.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the coach physically in the middle of the balance.

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, sitting beside a young engineer, looking at the engineer instead of the laptop full of code between them

storyboard.claim: Campbell was not there to review code; he coached management.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell beside an engineer, watching the person, not the screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Clarifies what the coach's role was not.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows his attention is on people rather than software.

image.subject: a manager and a team member sitting across a desk from each other, both relaxed, hands open on the desk, talking in a quiet office

storyboard.claim: Management must be built on trust, not just authority.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Manager and team member talking openly across a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the kind of management the previous line called for.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows trust as an open, two-way conversation.

storyboard.claim: After accepting management, leaders must destroy the ego that comes with the title.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text only: the next obstacle is ego.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from accepting management to the harder problem.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names ego as the next obstacle.

image.subject: a lone tech executive in a dark sweater standing on a stage in front of a dark empty auditorium, a single spotlight on him, arms folded, the rest of the seats in shadow

storyboard.claim: The industry culturally worships the ego-driven manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lone executive on a stage, admired from the dark seats.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the ego is hard to remove.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the stage as the place where the ego is rewarded.

image.subject: a tense glass-walled boardroom where a man stands at the head of the table, back to the camera, pointing at the team seated along the table, who look down at their laptops in silence

storyboard.claim: The archetype of the screaming visionary tyrant who changes the world.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A boss pointing while the team looks down.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the archetype a scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the cost to the team of this archetype.

storyboard.claim: A question leads into the vivid scene the book describes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text only: how did Bill Campbell tackle the ego problem.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the archetype to a concrete case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the date of the scene: August 2008.

image.subject: a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer walks into a conference room where a stocky white-haired man in his sixties sits at the head of a wooden table, the late 2000s, plain office

storyboard.claim: Jonathan Rosenberg walks into Bill Campbell's conference room in August 2008.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rosenberg entering; Campbell seated at the table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins the scene the question promised.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the two men in the room together.

image.subject: a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer, grinning from ear to ear and holding a printed paper article in both hands, standing in a conference room doorway, the late 2000s

storyboard.claim: Rosenberg is delighted and holds a printed copy of a Gawker article.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rosenberg grinning with a printed article.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the object the scene turns on.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows Rosenberg's pride in the printed piece.

storyboard.claim: The article's headline is the 10 most terrible tyrants of tech.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text only: the printed headline.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals what the printout says.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the exact headline of the article.

image.subject: a magazine spread in black and white with a row of stern portraits of tech executives in plain shirts and blazers, each one staring straight ahead, a bold layout modeled on a famous ad campaign

storyboard.claim: The article parodies Apple's Think Different ad, praising the tyrants instead of the crazy ones.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A parody layout of stern executive portraits.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows what the printout looks like.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the parody the narration describes.

image.subject: a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer leaning back in his office chair with a broad satisfied grin, reading a printed article spread across his desk

storyboard.claim: Rosenberg is on the list of tyrants.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rosenberg reading his own name in print, pleased.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Confirms that Rosenberg appears in the parody.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows his satisfaction with being named.

left.label: STEVE JOBS
left.subject: a slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, intense focused gaze

right.label: ROSENBERG
right.subject: a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer, engaged and conversational

storyboard.claim: Rosenberg is listed alongside Steve Jobs and Steve Ballmer.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jobs and Rosenberg as two entries on the same list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains who else made the list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts Rosenberg beside the famous names.

image.subject: a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer standing proudly in a glass office beside a trophy on a shelf, chin up, arms relaxed, the picture of a man who thinks he has made it

storyboard.claim: Rosenberg sees the list as proof he is a tough executive who has arrived.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rosenberg proud beside a trophy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains Rosenberg's reading of the list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Adds the trophy as the symbol of his pride.

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, looking down without smiling at a printed sheet slid across a wooden conference table toward him

storyboard.claim: Rosenberg slides the printout across the table; Campbell does not smile.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell, unsmiling, looking at the paper on the table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from Rosenberg's pride to Campbell's reaction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the printed article reaching the coach.

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, leaning forward over a conference table with a serious stare fixed on a man in a light blazer across from him

storyboard.claim: Campbell rebukes Rosenberg harshly and then asks a grounding question.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell leaning forward, stare fixed on Rosenberg.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the confrontation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the intensity of the rebuke and the turn to a question.

storyboard.claim: Campbell asks what Rosenberg's mother would think.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text only: the quoted question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the question the previous beat set up.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the exact question as a quotation.

image.subject: a manager with her hand resting on the shoulder of a team member seated at a desk in a quiet office, both looking down at the same screen, a moment of care

storyboard.claim: A leader's top priority is the well-being of their people.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager's hand on a team member's shoulder.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the story into the leadership lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the priority as a physical gesture of care.

image.subject: a team of engineers gathered around a laptop in a bright open office, relaxed and laughing together, no one standing over the others

storyboard.claim: Leaders must stop idolizing the toxic screaming tech tyrant.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A relaxed team laughing around a laptop.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the tyrant archetype with a healthy team.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the alternative to the tyrant.

storyboard.claim: Ask whether daily behavior creates support, respect and trust.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text only: three checks for daily behavior.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the lesson into questions for the viewer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives three concrete tests of a manager's daily behavior.

image.subject: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, pausing with a reflective expression, as if imagining a parent watching

storyboard.claim: If your mother would not be proud of how you speak to employees, you are failing as a manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager pausing, reflective, across from a colleague.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the mother test as a self-check.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the reflective pause that the test asks for.

image.subject: a bright open office with engineers working freely at standing desks in sunlight from tall windows, relaxed and absorbed in their own work, nobody watching over them

storyboard.claim: Great people flourish where their energy is liberated, not feared.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Free, absorbed engineers in a bright office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the principle behind the lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows what a liberated environment looks like.

image.subject: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, hunched at a desk in a dim corner, glancing nervously toward a closed glass office door

storyboard.claim: Fear stifles energy and makes people play it safe.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An employee glancing nervously at a closed door.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the cost of fear the previous line named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the fear a visible posture.

storyboard.claim: How do you institutionalize that kind of humanization among hard-charging executives?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text only: the practical question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the practical question after the philosophy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the next section as a process question.

image.subject: a man in his fifties with short graying hair and a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, measured and attentive, seated at the head of a long conference table in a glass-walled office, a clock on the wall

storyboard.claim: Campbell gave executives a process to force empathy into the room.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Eric Schmidt at the head of the table in a glass office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with a system.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the Monday meeting with Schmidt as its leader.

image.subject: a long conference table in a glass-walled Silicon Valley office with a dozen executives gathered around it, laptops closed in front of them, the most important meeting of the week

storyboard.claim: The Monday executive staff meeting gathers the company's most powerful people.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A dozen executives around a long table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the scene for the meeting described.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the size and weight of the meeting.

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, leaning toward a man in his fifties with short graying hair and a dark blazer, the two in quiet conversation at a table

storyboard.claim: Campbell coached Schmidt on how to open these meetings.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell coaching Schmidt across a table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows who coached whom.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the coaching in a private conversation.

image.subject: a large wall screen showing a world map covered in red pins, a man in a dark blazer with short graying hair pointing at the pins while executives watch from the table

storyboard.claim: The meeting opens with a Google map where executives drop pins on cities they visited.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A map screen covered in pins, with a presenter pointing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the opening ritual.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the map as the opening of the meeting.

storyboard.claim: The executives give what they call trip reports.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text only: the phrase trip reports.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the ritual the map leads to.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the ritual its official name.

image.subject: a group of executives laughing at a conference table, a kiteboard leaning against the wall behind them and a golf bag beside the door, relaxed and easy

storyboard.claim: Meetings open with weekend stories: kiteboarding, golf, engineering talk.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Laughing executives beside a kiteboard and golf bag.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the weekend talk the previous beat named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Adds concrete props for the weekend stories.

image.subject: a young boy in a soccer jersey kicking a ball across a sunny green field while a parent watches from the sideline, a light and easy weekend scene

storyboard.claim: Meetings also include updates on a manager's kids playing soccer.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A child kicking a soccer ball on a sunny field.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds a family detail to the weekend talk.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows a personal life update as a picture.

left.label: WEEKEND TALK
left.subject: a relaxed group chatting on a sunny golf course, bright and easy

right.label: CRISIS
right.subject: an office with a sharply falling red chart on the wall and tense faces around a table

storyboard.claim: During a stressful period, weekend talk would backfire.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Relaxed weekend talk versus a tense crisis room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the devil's advocate objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the two situations the objection compares.

image.subject: a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer sitting at a conference table with arms folded and a skeptical frown, looking across at a colleague

storyboard.claim: Talking about a weekend trip feels like denial to a manager facing the business reality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A skeptical executive with arms folded.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the objection a face.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the skepticism the objection carries.

image.subject: a manager at a desk staring intently at a spreadsheet on a laptop screen, a stack of printed reports beside the keyboard, every minute of the day apparently spent on numbers

storyboard.claim: An amateur manager thinks every second must go to a spreadsheet, but the team time is calculated.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager fixed on a spreadsheet.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the view the previous objection came from.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the spreadsheet mindset being contrasted.
